prompt: Match each term to what it is.

pairs.right: A measurement, such as the share of requests answered
An internal target for that measurement
A contract with a customer, with credits

right_distractors: A guarantee that the service will stay up

prompt: A hosting contract promises 99.9% availability. What does that clause amount to?
hint: What happens when it is missed?

choices.text: A guarantee the site will be up
choices.why: Nothing in it stops an outage; it says what happens after one.

choices.text: A price, paid in credits, for falling short
choices.why: Right. And the credit is capped at the fee.

choices.text: Insurance for the customer's lost sales
choices.why: The credit is a fraction of the hosting fee, not of the customer's losses.

choices.text: A measurement of the service
choices.why: That is the SLI; the SLA is the contract built on one.

prompt: Why does a team set its SLO tighter than the SLA it has signed?
hint: An alarm has to ring before the fire.

choices.text: To be warned while the contract still holds
choices.why: Right. Missing 99.95% is a warning; missing 99.9% is a breach.

choices.text: Customers read the SLO and expect it
choices.why: The SLO is internal; customers see the SLA.

choices.text: A tighter SLO lowers the credits owed
choices.why: Credits come from the SLA, whatever the SLO says.

choices.text: Measurement is less precise inside the company
choices.why: The margin is for time to act, not for measurement error.

prompt: A provider's SLA counts only complete unreachability, measured by its own monitoring. For three hours your site takes 30 seconds to answer each page. Are you owed a credit?

choices.text: Yes, three hours breaks 99.9%
choices.why: Three hours would, if they counted; by this contract they do not.

choices.text: Yes, if you can prove slowness
choices.why: Slowness is not in the definition, so no proof of it helps.

choices.text: No: by that definition the site was up
choices.why: Right. It answered, slowly. The fine print is the promise.

choices.text: For the hours outside maintenance windows
choices.why: None of it counts, maintenance or not: the site answered.

prompt: Two SLAs both say 99.9%. Which of these can make them promise different things? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The window: calendar month or rolling 30 days
choices.why: Right. A rolling window never forgets a bad week.

choices.text: What counts as down
choices.why: Right. Unreachable only, or errors and slowness too.

choices.text: The list of exclusions
choices.why: Right. Announced maintenance and beta features can remove the hours that matter.

choices.text: Whether the provider uses VRRP or HSRP
choices.why: How the provider builds it is its own business; the contract defines the result.

choices.text: Where the measurement is taken
choices.why: Right. Inside the provider's network, or where a customer stands.

prompt: How many minutes of downtime does an objective of 99.9% allow over a 30-day month?
Lesson 14 gave 43.80 minutes a month for 99.9%, and this lesson gives 43.20. Which is right?

choices.text: 43.80: the later figure has a rounding error
choices.why: Both are exact for the month each one assumed.

choices.text: Both, for two different months
choices.why: Right. A twelfth of 365 days against 30 days; an SLA has to say which.

choices.text: 43.20: lesson 14 counted leap years
choices.why: Lesson 14 used a year of 365 days, not a leap year.

choices.text: Neither: availability is a yearly figure
choices.why: Contracts measure by month all the time; the window is theirs to choose.

prompt: A service promises 99.9% a month. One night a person is paged and restores the service by hand in 45 minutes. What has that done to the month?

choices.text: Used about a tenth of the budget
choices.why: 45 minutes is more than the whole 43.20.

choices.text: Nothing, since the service came back the same night
choices.why: Coming back is what ends the spending; the 45 minutes are spent.

choices.text: Spent more than its whole budget alone
choices.why: Right. One incident that waits for a person spends more than the month allows.

choices.text: Used the same as 794 failovers
choices.why: 794 failovers of 3.264 s are 43.2 minutes; this is more.

prompt: Every deployment carries some risk of downtime, so an objective of 100% amounts to a promise never to ___ anything.
What does the RTO measure?
hint: It looks forward from the incident.

choices.text: How much data may be lost
choices.why: That is the RPO, which looks backwards.

choices.text: How long the service may be down
choices.why: Right. From the incident until the service is back.

choices.text: How often the system fails in a year
choices.why: That is closer to MTBF, lesson 14.

choices.text: How long it takes to repair the broken part
choices.why: Repair can take far longer; the service may come back elsewhere first.

prompt: A backup runs at 01:00 every night. The primary's disk dies at 22:30 the same day, and the backup is restored. How many hours of writes are lost?
hint: From the last good copy to the incident.

prompt: In lesson 16 lb1 stayed broken until somebody restarted it, yet the RTO was 2.694 s. Why is the RTO not the time until lb1 was fixed?

choices.text: When the service is back
choices.why: Right. On any machine: lb2 carried the service, and the repair of lb1 is a separate clock.

choices.text: lb1 was fixed within 2.694 s
choices.why: Nothing restarted lb1's HAProxy in that time.

choices.text: The RTO only counts network time
choices.why: It counts all of it; the lab's network had no delay anyway.

choices.text: A balancer has no RTO, only an RPO
choices.why: Every service has an RTO; this one was measured.

prompt: A database has a synchronous replica and a nightly backup. Somebody deletes a table by mistake at 15:00. What is the RPO for this failure?
hint: What does the replica hold a moment later?

choices.text: Zero, thanks to the synchronous replica
choices.why: The replica received the deletion as faithfully as any write.

choices.text: The replication lag, a few seconds
choices.why: A synchronous replica has no lag, and it deleted the table too.

choices.text: Back to last night's backup, for that table
choices.why: Right. Only a copy taken before the mistake has the rows.

choices.text: None: a deletion is not a failure
choices.why: Losing a table is exactly the failure backups exist for.

prompt: Lesson 14's program gave the lab's design, with a single ISP link and DNS server, 99.79990%. Sales wants to sign 99.9%. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: 99.8 rounds to 99.9
choices.why: 1051.7 minutes against 525.6 is a factor of two, not rounding.

choices.text: Its own arithmetic breaks it
choices.why: Right. It predicts about twice the downtime the promise allows.

choices.text: Balancers and web servers need more twins
choices.why: They are already redundant; the single serial parts set the ceiling.

choices.text: 99.9% needs HSRP rather than VRRP
choices.why: The protocol is not the constraint; the single ISP link and DNS server are.

prompt: A shop promises its customers 99.99% while its database provider promises 99.9%. The provider misses by an hour. Why do the credits not balance?
hint: Whose fee is each credit a fraction of?

choices.text: The provider owes nothing for an hour
choices.why: An hour misses 99.9% a month, so a credit is owed.

choices.text: The credits are equal, so they cancel
choices.why: They are fractions of two different bills.

choices.text: They are cut from different bills
choices.why: Right. The shop receives part of one fee and owes part of many, having promised more than it bought.

choices.text: Credits apply from 99.99% upwards
choices.why: Any SLA can carry credits.

prompt: Why does a promise above about 99.9% a month require every common failure to be handled automatically?
hint: Compare a person's response time with 21.60 minutes.

choices.text: Automation is cheaper than staff
choices.why: Perhaps, but the reason here is the clock, not the cost.

choices.text: One wait for a person spends the budget
choices.why: Right. 21.60 minutes at 99.95% leaves no room for a night call.

choices.text: Contracts forbid manual recovery
choices.why: They say nothing of how; the number decides.

choices.text: People cause more failures than machines
choices.why: Maybe so, but the argument is about recovery time, not cause.

prompt: Put the steps of a failover drill in order.
items: Pick a calm afternoon and tell the people watching
Start measuring, with a ping or a request loop
Read the gap from the timestamps
Compare the gap with the promise and write it down
trap: The measurement has to be running before the failure, or the gap is never seen.

prompt: What makes a replica synchronous?
hint: When does the primary confirm a write?

choices.text: It copies the data once a night
choices.why: That is a backup.

choices.text: It sits in the same rack as the primary, close by
choices.why: Placement is a separate choice; it can be anywhere the distance allows.

choices.text: The primary waits for it before confirming
choices.why: Right. So nothing confirmed is lost, and every write pays a round trip.

choices.text: It replays the changes a few seconds later
choices.why: That is asynchronous replication, with a lag.

prompt: Light in fibre covers about 200 km a millisecond. How many milliseconds does a synchronous replica 1000 km away add to every write, for the round trip?
An asynchronous replica is promoted after the primary dies during the busiest hour of the day. What has been lost?
hint: The primary confirmed before it copied.

choices.text: Nothing, since replication is continuous
choices.why: Continuous is not instant: the replica runs behind.

choices.text: Confirmed writes the replica had not received
choices.why: Right. The lag at that moment, and a busy hour makes it longer.

choices.text: Everything since last night's backup
choices.why: The replica has everything up to its lag.

choices.text: Writes still in progress in the application
choices.why: Writes already confirmed to users are lost too, which is the painful part.

prompt: The primary is cut off from the network but still running, and the replica is promoted. Both accept writes. Which mechanism from lesson 14 prevents this?
hint: Who may act, and making sure the other has stopped.

choices.text: A shorter heartbeat interval
choices.why: Faster detection makes the promotion happen sooner, split brain included.

choices.text: Quorum, with fencing of the old one
choices.why: Right. A third vote decides who may be primary, and fencing stops the other.

choices.text: Synchronous replication
choices.why: It keeps copies equal while they are connected; the problem starts when they are not.

choices.text: A nightly backup
choices.why: A backup recovers data afterwards; it does not stop two writers.

prompt: A clinic's booking system promises 99.95% a month. It runs on one database server with a nightly backup, and a restore takes three hours. Can it keep the promise?

choices.text: Yes, if the server never fails
choices.why: A promise that holds only when nothing breaks is not an availability promise.

choices.text: No, one restore breaks it
choices.why: Right. 180 minutes against 21.60, eight months' budget in one night; the design needs automatic failover.

choices.text: Yes, because backups give an RPO of zero
choices.why: A nightly backup gives an RPO of up to a day, and the RTO is the problem here.

choices.text: It depends on the credit table
choices.why: Credits say what a miss costs, not whether the design can avoid one.

prompt: A company wants an RPO of zero for orders and a copy 3000 km away in case the whole region is lost. Why is one synchronous replica 3000 km away a poor way to get both?
hint: 200 km a millisecond, there and back.

choices.text: Synchronous replicas stay within one region
choices.why: They can; the cost is the time, not a rule.

choices.text: It would lose orders during the round trip
choices.why: Synchronous loses nothing confirmed; it is slow, not lossy.

choices.text: It protects against deleted tables too well
choices.why: It copies deletions as well; it does not protect against them at all.

choices.text: Every order would wait about 30 ms longer
choices.why: Right. A synchronous replica nearby for the RPO, and an asynchronous one far away for the region, is the usual answer.
